title: The dual coordinate Hopf algebra represents finite-group characters
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], and let $G$ be a finite commutative $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme]. Put $H=\Gamma(G,\mathcal O_G)$ and use its coordinate Hopf structure [def-sfb-affine-coordinate-hopf-algebra]. The vector space $H^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(H,k)$ has a commutative Hopf algebra structure obtained by transposing the structure maps of $H$: its multiplication is the transpose of the comultiplication of $H$, its unit is the transpose of the counit, its comultiplication is the transpose of multiplication, its counit is the transpose of the unit, and its antipode is the transpose of the antipode. Use the finite-dimensional identification $(H\otimes_kH)^*=H^*\otimes_kH^*$. The finite commutative group scheme $G^D=\operatorname{Spec}(H^*)$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] represents the character functor: for every $k$-scheme $T$ [def-pc-scheme] there is a canonical bijection of groups
$$\operatorname{Hom}_k(T,G^D)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{T\text{-grp}}(G\times_kT,\mathbf G_{m,T}),$$
natural in $T$, where $\mathbf G_m$ is the multiplicative group [def-sc-gm-ga] and multiplication on the right is pointwise multiplication. Its coordinate vector space is exactly $H^*$, not the space of functions on geometric points. No perfection or invertibility of $\dim_kH$ is assumed.

source.place: Section 11c, printed pp.212–214: Lemma 11.11, construction preceding Theorem 11.12, and Theorem 11.12. The scheme-valued form is the Zariski gluing of the functor on all test algebras.

proof.text: Finite coordinates. By [def-sc-group-scheme], $G=\operatorname{Spec}H$ with $H$ finite-dimensional. Choose a finite basis $(h_i)$: from a finite spanning list discard a vector whenever it is in the span of the others, leaving an independent spanning list. Let $(h_i^*)$ be its dual basis and put $D=H^*$. The evaluation map $H\to D^*$ is an isomorphism: its inverse sends $F$ to $\sum_iF(h_i^*)h_i$. Thus evaluation detects equality. By [lem-sfb-finite-free-tensor-dual] identify $(H\otimes H)^*$ with $D\otimes D$, with pairing $\langle f\otimes g,a\otimes b\rangle=f(a)g(b)$; iterating gives the same assertion for three or four factors. By [lem-sfb-linear-dual-dimension-rank], $D$ is finite-dimensional of dimension $\dim_k H$. Write $\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon,S$ for the coordinate operations of [def-sfb-affine-coordinate-hopf-algebra]. Define $\mu_D=\Delta^*$, $\eta_D=\epsilon^*$, $\Delta_D=\mu^*$, $\epsilon_D=\eta^*$ and $S_D=S^*$ using these identifications.

source.place: §11c, printed pp.212–213, construction, Lemma 11.11 and proof of Theorem 11.12; §4g, printed p.92, character/group-like calculation.

proof.text: Transpose the algebra and coalgebra identities. In evaluation notation $(fg)(h)=(f\otimes g)(\Delta h)$, $1_D(h)=\epsilon(h)$, $\langle\Delta_Df,a\otimes b\rangle=f(ab)$ and $\epsilon_D(f)=f(1)$. For $f,g,l\in D$, the evaluations of $(fg)l$ and $f(gl)$ on $h$ are respectively $(f\otimes g\otimes l)((\Delta\otimes1)\Delta h)$ and $(f\otimes g\otimes l)((1\otimes\Delta)\Delta h)$; they agree. The two unit identities similarly are the two counit identities of $H$. Conversely, evaluating the two iterated coproducts of $f$ on $a\otimes b\otimes c$ gives $f((ab)c)=f(a(bc))$; their counit identities give $f(1a)=f(a)=f(a1)$. Since $G$ is commutative, its multiplication is fixed by swapping factors, hence $\Delta=\tau\Delta$ by the coordinate definition, so $fg=gf$. Since $ab=ba$ in $H$, $\Delta_D$ is also fixed by the swap. All tensor equalities are detected by the finite tensor pairings of [lem-sfb-finite-free-tensor-dual].

source.place: §11c, printed pp.212–213, construction, Lemma 11.11 and proof of Theorem 11.12; §4g, printed p.92, character/group-like calculation.

proof.text: Check the bialgebra compatibility, rather than assuming that transposition preserves it. Write $\Delta a=\sum a_1\otimes a_2$ and $\Delta b=\sum b_1\otimes b_2$. The evaluations on $a\otimes b$ of $\Delta_D(fg)$ and $\Delta_D(f)\Delta_D(g)$ are both $\sum f(a_1b_1)g(a_2b_2)$: for the first use $\Delta(ab)=\Delta(a)\Delta(b)$, and for the second use $\langle\Delta_Df,u\otimes v\rangle=f(uv)$. Also $\Delta_D(1_D)(a,b)=\epsilon(ab)=\epsilon(a)\epsilon(b)$ and $\epsilon_D(fg)=(f\otimes g)\Delta(1)=f(1)g(1)$, with $\epsilon_D(1_D)=1$. Thus $\Delta_D$ and $\epsilon_D$ are unital algebra maps. Here tensor multiplication is precisely $(f\otimes g)(l\otimes q)=fl\otimes gq$ from [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property]; evaluation detects the asserted equalities by [lem-sfb-finite-free-tensor-dual].

source.place: §11c, printed pp.212–213, construction, Lemma 11.11 and proof of Theorem 11.12; §4g, printed p.92, character/group-like calculation.

proof.text: The transposed antipode. Evaluate $\mu_D(S_D\otimes1)\Delta_Df$ at $h$ to obtain $f(\sum S(h_1)h_2)=f(1)\epsilon(h)$; the other antipode identity gives $f(\sum h_1S(h_2))=f(1)\epsilon(h)$. Both are $\eta_D\epsilon_D(f)$. Moreover inversion in a commutative group commutes with multiplication: the product of the two inverses multiplies the product of the two elements to the identity. Applied to the group-scheme diagrams, this yields $\Delta S=(S\otimes S)\Delta$ and $\epsilon S=\epsilon$. Consequently $S_D(fg)(h)=(f\otimes g)\Delta(S h)=(S_Df\otimes S_Dg)\Delta h$, and $S_D(1_D)=1_D$. This proves that $D$ has the required commutative Hopf algebra structure with exactly the six transposed operations. Applying [lem-sfb-hopf-spectrum-functor] gives its affine group scheme $G^D=\operatorname{Spec}D$. It is commutative because $\Delta_D$ is fixed by the swap. It is finite by [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], since $D$ is finite-dimensional. Its global coordinate algebra is $D$ by [def-weil-affine-spectrum].

source.place: §11c, printed pp.212–213, construction, Lemma 11.11 and proof of Theorem 11.12; §4g, printed p.92, character/group-like calculation.

proof.text: Affine test algebras. Let $R$ be any commutative $k$-algebra, including nonreduced algebras, and put $H_R=H\otimes_kR$. The map $H_R\to\operatorname{Hom}_k(D,R)$ sends $h\otimes r$ to $(f\mapsto rf(h))$ and is bijective. The finite basis makes $D$ projective: lift each basis image through any surjective linear map and extend linearly. Indeed [lem-pc-finite-projective-module-tensor-hom] with $M=D$, $P=R$, $Q=k$, followed by the tensor unit and swap identifications and $D^*=H$, gives this map; alternatively its inverse is $\alpha\mapsto x_\alpha=\sum_i h_i\otimes\alpha(h_i^*)$. Direct substitution in both composites gives the identity by the two dual-basis expansion formulas. A linear map $\alpha:D\to R$ is a unital algebra map exactly when $\Delta_R(x_\alpha)=x_\alpha\otimes_Rx_\alpha$ and $\epsilon_R(x_\alpha)=1$: pairing the first equation with $f\otimes g$ gives $\alpha(fg)=\alpha(f)\alpha(g)$, and pairing the second gives $\alpha(1_D)=1$. These pairings detect equality over $R$ as well, because the tensors of the displayed basis are an $R$-basis. By [def-weil-affine-spectrum], the algebra maps $\alpha$ are precisely the $R$-points of $G^D$.

source.place: §11c, printed pp.212–213, construction, Lemma 11.11 and proof of Theorem 11.12; §4g, printed p.92, character/group-like calculation.

proof.text: Characters on an affine test. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], $G_R=\operatorname{Spec}(H_R)$. For a group-like $x\in H_R$, the two antipode equations evaluated at $x$ give $S_R(x)x=xS_R(x)=1$. Hence the formula $\sum_n r_nt^n\mapsto\sum_n r_nx^n$ defines an $R$-algebra map $R[t,t^{-1}]\to H_R$ (the sums are finite). It is the unique such map with $t\mapsto x$, because $t^{-1}$ must map to $x^{-1}$. The coordinate operations of $\mathbf G_m$ in [def-sc-gm-ga] show this is a group morphism $\chi_x:G_R\to\mathbf G_{m,R}$: multiplication and identity are exactly $\Delta_Rx=x\otimes x$ and $\epsilon_Rx=1$, while inversion is $S_Rx=x^{-1}$. Conversely a character has a coordinate map with $t$-image satisfying these equations. This uses [def-weil-affine-spectrum] on affine sources and [def-pc-fibre-product] to regard a map to $\mathbf G_m$ together with the structure map as a map over $\operatorname{Spec}R$. Thus $\alpha\mapsto\chi_{x_\alpha}$ is bijective, with inverse $\alpha(f)=\langle f,x\rangle$.

source.place: §11c, printed pp.212–213, construction, Lemma 11.11 and proof of Theorem 11.12; §4g, printed p.92, character/group-like calculation.

proof.text: Group law and algebra naturality. For two algebra maps $\alpha,\beta:D\to R$, multiplication of the associated $G^D(R)$-points is $\alpha\star\beta=\mu_R(\alpha\otimes\beta)\Delta_D$ by [lem-sfb-hopf-spectrum-functor]. Since $\langle\Delta_Df,a\otimes b\rangle=f(ab)$, its associated tensor is $x_{\alpha\star\beta}=x_\alpha x_\beta$. The character with this tensor is $\chi_{x_\alpha}\chi_{x_\beta}$, because on every $R$-algebra $B$ and $g\in G(B)$ its value is $g^*(x_\alpha x_\beta)=g^*(x_\alpha)g^*(x_\beta)$. The identity has tensor $1_H\otimes1_R$ and gives the constant character $1$; thus the bijection is a group isomorphism. For any $k$-algebra map $u:R\to R'$ the formula $x_{u\alpha}=\sum_i h_i\otimes u(\alpha(h_i^*))=(1\otimes u)x_\alpha$ proves compatibility with base change, as does the Laurent formula for $\chi_x$. This includes restriction to every affine open of an affine test scheme.

source.place: §11c, printed pp.212–213, construction, Lemma 11.11 and proof of Theorem 11.12; §4g, printed p.92, character/group-like calculation.

proof.text: Forward extension to all schemes. Let $T$ be any $k$-scheme and $f:T\to G^D$ a $k$-map. Choose an affine open cover $U_i=\operatorname{Spec}R_i$ of $T$. The affine construction gives $\chi_i:G\times U_i\to\mathbf G_m$. On each affine open $W\subset U_i\cap U_j$, the two restrictions have the same tensor by algebra naturality; these $W$ need not equal the intersection. Thus their $t$-images agree on the open cover $(G\times W)$ of $G\times(U_i\cap U_j)$. The structure-sheaf separatedness axiom makes them equal there. The $t$-images, and their inverses, therefore glue to inverse global sections on $G\times T$. Substitution of these sections gives a $k$-algebra map $k[t,t^{-1}]\to\Gamma(G\times T,\mathcal O)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-into-affine-scheme] this is a unique map to $\mathbf G_m$. Pairing with the projection to $T$ using [def-pc-fibre-product] gives $\chi:G\times T\to\mathbf G_{m,T}$. Its group-morphism identities hold: locally on the cover by $U_i$ they are the established affine identities, and maps to the affine scheme $\mathbf G_m$ agree if their coordinate sections agree on a cover. The same reasoning proves independence of the cover.

source.place: Theorem 11.12, printed p.213, extended from affine tests using Stacks Tag 01I1 (lemma-morphism-into-affine) and the structure-sheaf gluing axiom. The explicit extension argument is supplied here.

proof.text: Inverse extension. For a $T$-group homomorphism $\chi:G\times T\to\mathbf G_{m,T}$, restriction to each affine $U_i$ gives the unique algebra map $\alpha_i:D\to R_i$ by the affine bijection. On every affine open $W\subset U_i\cap U_j$ the two restrictions of $\alpha_i$ agree, since their characters both equal $\chi|_W$. For each $f\in D$, the sections $\alpha_i(f)$ therefore glue to a unique section $\alpha(f)\in\Gamma(T,\mathcal O_T)$. Addition, multiplication, the unit, and the fixed $k$-scalars are preserved because they are preserved on every $U_i$, and the structure sheaf is separated. This gives a $k$-algebra map $D\to\Gamma(T,\mathcal O_T)$, hence a unique $k$-map $T\to\operatorname{Spec}D$ by [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-into-affine-scheme]. The two constructions are inverse since their restrictions to each $U_i$ are inverse and coordinate sections in an affine target are determined by their restrictions to this cover. This proves bijectivity for arbitrary $T$, including $T=\varnothing$, when all the morphism sets in question are singleton sets.

source.place: Theorem 11.12, printed p.213, extended from affine tests using Stacks Tag 01I1 (lemma-morphism-into-affine) and the structure-sheaf gluing axiom. The explicit extension argument is supplied here.

proof.text: Scheme naturality and the group assertion. Given any $k$-map $v:T'\to T$, cover $T$ by affine $U_i$ and each $v^{-1}U_i$ by affine opens $V_{ij}$. On $V_{ij}\to U_i$ the claimed base-change equality is exactly the algebra naturality already computed for $R_i\to\Gamma(V_{ij},\mathcal O)$. The affine-target uniqueness of [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-into-affine-scheme], applied to the coordinate sections, then proves the equality on $T'$. Pointwise multiplication of two characters and multiplication of two $G^D(T)$-points likewise agree after restriction to every $U_i$ by the computed affine group law; separatedness of coordinate sections gives equality globally. The resulting bijection is therefore canonical, natural in all test schemes, and an isomorphism of groups. The construction used the full dual vector space and the full rings $H\otimes R$ throughout. No geometric-point replacement, perfection, reducedness, or division by $\dim_kH$ occurred.
